source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task (Exp 1)
finding: People who saw three example toys or creatures copied the example features into their own new designs more than people who saw none. The number of ideas did not change.
numbers: Exp 1, N=94 (44 control, 50 examples). Overall conformity toys .22 control vs .35 examples, F(1,92)=8.13. Creatures .11 vs .24, F(1,92)=12.50. Ideas per person about 2.8-3.1 in both arms (F<1.1).
limits: Intro psychology students, group sessions, toy and creature tasks only. The copied features were chosen by the experimenters. Effect is on features, not on number of ideas.
agent_relevance: Shown examples pull outputs toward the example's features even when the task asks for novelty. Measure feature copying, not just idea count, when testing whether our agent is anchored on a prior output.

source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task (Exp 2, delay and order)
finding: Conformity did not fade when the examples were shown earlier and testing came later. The effect held for the second task as well as the first.
numbers: Exp 2, N=91. Toy overall conformity: control .21 (first) and .16 (second); examples .31 (immediate) and .32 (delayed). Conformity x order interaction F(1,87)=.36, not significant. Order x conformity was significant only for the electronics feature, F(1,87)=5.66 (larger effect after delay).
limits: Delay was only minutes, within one session. No effect of order on any measure.
agent_relevance: A shown output keeps its pull after other material intervenes. Pushing a prior attempt out of the recent context by one step is not enough on its own.

source: Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) Constraining effects of examples in a creative generation task (Exp 3, biasing instructions)
finding: Telling people to make ideas very different from the examples did not remove the copying. Telling them to resemble the examples raised it. So copying is not mainly a polite guess about what the experimenter wants.
numbers: Exp 3, N=80, 20 per arm, creatures. Overall conformity: control .16, standard examples .25, diverge instruction .33, conform instruction .44. ANOVA F(3,76)=8.69. Control vs the three example groups t(76)=3.82. Standard vs diverge not different, t(76)=1.33. Tail feature F(3,76)=9.27.
limits: The diverge arm was numerically higher than standard, so the instruction did not help at all in this study. Contrast with Chrysikou and Weisberg (2005), where an instruction not to copy did help (see b07).
agent_relevance: A plain instruction 'do not copy the example' is weak evidence of defixation. Our test (question b in SUBFIELDS) needs a code-measured copy rate, not the model's own claim.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity (Exp 1)
finding: Replicated the conformity effect, with a dose response: more examples gave more copying. But total output, elaborateness and non-critical features were not reduced, so copying did not shrink creativity in this paradigm.
numbers: Exp 1, N=80, five groups with increasing numbers of examples. Conformity rose with number of examples: omnibus F(4,75)=5.91, linear trend F(1,75)=4.75. Number of creatures and elaboration: F<1. Control and three-example arms matched Smith et al. 1993 closely.
limits: Conformity was measured on experimenter-chosen critical features. Authors say copying 'may not actually constrain creativity'. The constraint claim is the contested part.
agent_relevance: Separate two claims: copying rises with example count (solid) and copying hurts outcome quality (not shown here). Our agent should log copy rate and quality separately. More examples in context = more copying.

source: Marsh, Landau and Hicks (1996) (Exp 2 and 3)
finding: Examples that bundled unusual feature pairs were rated more creative than natural pairs or no examples. A delay between examples and test increased conformity, as models of unconscious plagiarism predict.
numbers: Exp 2, N about 75: creativity rating 3.51 (SD .64) for artificial co-varying features vs 3.07 (natural) and 3.08 (control), F(2,72)=4.15. Exp 3, N=74: delay raised conformity (abstract; exact statistics not extracted).
limits: Exp 3 conflicts with the flat delay result in Smith et al. Exp 2 (b02). The two differ in delay length and design. Ratings came from 16 raters.
agent_relevance: Examples can help when they show a rare combination. Choose examples by how far they sit from the default, not only by how relevant they are. Delay may increase unwanted copying, not remove it.

source: Wang, Okada and Takagi (2023) How to effectively overcome fixation: a systematic review of fixation and defixation studies (instructions)
finding: Review of 53 experimental studies. Whether an instruction to avoid examples works depends on the source of fixation and the participants. It worked in a replication with psychology students tested alone, and failed with engineering students, professionals and groups. Naming the example in a warning can re-activate it.
numbers: 53 studies. Instruction not to copy: no effect in Jansson and Smith (1991), Viswanathan and Linsey (2013a,b), Viswanathan et al. (2014); relaxed fixation in Chrysikou and Weisberg (2005). Authors' two explanations: group vs individual testing, and psychology vs engineering domain knowledge.
limits: Narrative review without pooled effect sizes. Selection by authors' judgment. The domain-knowledge explanation is the authors' proposal, not tested.
agent_relevance: Instruction-only defixation is fragile. Expect it to fail when the model has strong domain priors. Treat 'do not copy' as a weak baseline arm.

source: George and Wiley (2020) Need something different? Effects of examples and task instructions on creative idea generation (Exp 1, verbal examples)
finding: Showing a list of common example uses together with a warning to avoid them raised originality on the Alternate Uses Task. Showing the same examples with no warning did nothing for originality and made people repeat the examples.
numbers: Exp 1, N=144 (2x2: examples vs none, avoid vs no avoid, df 140). Original ideas: main effect of examples F(1,140)=4.85 p=.030; of avoid F(1,140)=5.60 p=.019. Planned comparison on originality d=0.58. Proportion of original ideas, examples+avoid vs rest: d=0.51 (t(142)=2.65). Share of responses that repeat the examples: .27 (examples, no avoid) vs .06 others, d=1.17.
limits: Online AUT, 3 minute generation, verbal examples of common uses. The avoid list names exactly what to avoid. Unoriginal examples only.
agent_relevance: A named avoid-list works when the examples are the obvious ideas. This is a cheap defixation arm for the agent: list the already-tried attempts and say do not repeat them. Test it against no list, since list-without-warning backfires.

source: George and Wiley (2020) (Exp 2, visual examples)
finding: When the common examples were shown as pictures, originality fell, which is fixation. The avoid warning reduced the harm but did not lift originality above the no-example arm.
numbers: Exp 2, parallel design to Exp 1. Test statistics not extracted (abstract-level reading). Direction: visual examples reduced originality; avoid instruction mitigated but gave no gain over no examples.
limits: Abstract and design read; the Exp 2 test statistics were not recorded this session.
agent_relevance: Concrete, vivid prior outputs fixate more than a verbal list. Show a prior attempt as a short abstract description, not as full text, when asking for something different.

source: Wang, Okada and Takagi (2023) (abstraction and format of examples)
finding: Presenting examples at a higher level of abstraction, as a function tree or as expansive examples, reduced copying and raised originality. Adding a sketch back removed the benefit. One text-vs-picture result failed to replicate.
numbers: Atilola et al. (2016): function tree cut copied features with idea count unchanged, and quality rose; effect lost when a sketch was added. Ezzat et al. (2020): warning that names examples at a higher abstraction level cut fixation and raised originality. Agogue et al. (2014): expansive examples cut fixation. Cardoso and Badke-Schaub (2009a) found text beat picture; their 2009b replication found no difference.
limits: Numbers are reported only as directions in this review. Original sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Show the agent the structure or principle of a prior attempt, not its surface. The Ezzat result is the closest human analogue to 'avoid X, which is a kind of Y' and fits our abstraction operator.

source: Wang, Okada and Takagi (2023) (incubation, impasse, defixation vs quality)
finding: Incubation helps against fixation from misleading cues but not against fixation from domain knowledge (Wiley 1998). Switching tasks before an impasse reduced fixation and raised flexibility. Defixation does not guarantee better ideas: gains can come from within-frame work.
numbers: Wiley (1998): incubation helped misleading-information fixation, not domain-knowledge fixation. Lu et al. (2017): switch task before impasse reduced fixation. Smith et al. (2017): switch task raised novelty for a flexible category, not a stable one. Segal (2004): effect independent of interval length.
limits: Review level only. Open-ended problems have no clear impasse signal, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Supports our G1 (act on a signal): the impasse detector, not a clock, should trigger the shift. Also warns that a reduction in copying is not proof of a better answer. Check quality separately.

source: Purcell and Gero (1996) Design and other types of fixation, as reported by Wang et al. 2023
finding: An example built on mechanical engineering knowledge fixated only the students who knew mechanical engineering. Fixation depends on what the person already knows.
numbers: No participant numbers or effect sizes extracted. Reported as a supporting case in the 2023 review.
limits: Secondhand: the original paper was not opened, only the review's account of it.
agent_relevance: Fixation scales with prior knowledge of the domain. A strong model with deep priors in a domain may be more fixated by on-topic examples, not less. Test per domain.

source: Purcell, Williams, Gero and Colbron (1993), as summarised in a web search result
finding: Attempts to replicate Jansson and Smith's fixation effect were largely unsuccessful. Apparent fixation in some conditions tracked familiarity with existing examples of the problem, and differed by discipline and experience.
numbers: No numbers seen. Search-result text only.
limits: Not opened: only a search snippet. Treat as a lead to verify.
agent_relevance: A mixed replication record means the human effect is context dependent. Report LLM results with the same care and do not assume them from the human result.

source: Sio, Kotovsky and Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes
finding: Meta-analysis of 43 design studies. Examples narrowed the search (less variety) but ideas were more novel and higher in quality. Gains were larger with fewer and less common examples. One uncommon example helped most.
numbers: 43 studies. Effect sizes not obtained: the paper could not be opened (HTTP 403, PDF behind a wall). Findings come from a search summary of the abstract and highlights.
limits: NOT OPENED. Direction of findings unverified until the paper is read. It conflicts with a pure 'examples = fixation' view, so it is the key paper to check next.
agent_relevance: If this holds, the right question is which examples to show, not whether to show any. A single rare example may beat none. Test: zero vs one common vs one rare example in the agent's open mode.

source: McCaffrey (2012) Innovation relies on the obscure (generic parts technique), via Association for Psychological Science press release
finding: Teaching people to break each object into parts and ask whether the description of a part implies a use raised solution rates on insight problems that need an obscure feature of an object.
numbers: Eight problems. Trained group solved them '67 percent more often', and solved more than 8 of 10. Control rate, sample sizes and experiment number are not given in the release. A secondary write-up gave about 50% vs 83% (unverified).
limits: Press release only; the Psychological Science paper (HTTP 403) was not opened. The 67% is a relative gain. Lab puzzles. Works when the obscure part is known but described in a use-implying way.
agent_relevance: The generic parts step is a cheap re-description operator: rewrite each object or term in use-free words, then re-ask. It maps to our reframe operator and can be code-forced. Needs a real test on our puzzles before adoption.

source: Sio and Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review, as reported in Gilhooly (2016)
finding: Across 117 studies, setting a problem aside gives a small positive effect. It is larger for divergent tasks, larger with an undemanding task in the gap, and larger after a longer first attempt.
numbers: 117 studies, mean d=0.29. Gilhooly's text: benefits greater with an undemanding interpolated task than with a demanding one or none.
limits: Effect size read from Gilhooly's summary, not the original. Small effect, many task types pooled. Applies to people with memory decay and mind wandering.
agent_relevance: A mean d of 0.29 is the right prior for a break: small. An LLM does not forget, so the closest analogue is a context reset or a changed frame, not waiting.

source: Ricks, Turley-Ames and Wiley (2007) Effects of working memory capacity on mental set due to domain knowledge
finding: More working memory helped on remote-associate items in general, but not when a misleading answer was strongly activated by domain knowledge. High capacity plus strong prior knowledge could make the set worse.
numbers: High-baseball-knowledge participants: working memory score unrelated to performance on baseball-misleading items; positively related on neutral items. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Remote Associates Task only. Baseball knowledge as the source of fixation. The attention-breadth interpretation is the authors'.
agent_relevance: A stronger, more focused reasoner can lock harder onto a wrong frame. Do not assume a more capable model needs less defixation. Check capability x fixation in our own runs.

source: German and Defeyter (2000) Immunity to functional fixedness in young children
finding: On a Duncker-style box task, 6 and 7 year olds were slowed when the box had been shown holding things. 5 year olds were not slowed at all.
numbers: N=60 (30 per condition, ten per age group). Older children solved with box as support in 18% when its container use was shown vs 89% when not. 5 year olds 64% vs 65%. Seven-year-old difference Fisher p=.04. Authors cite a companion study, total N=100, with the same pattern.
limits: Tiny cells (n=10). A box-shelf analogue of the candle problem, not the original. The age effect is interpreted as developing intuitions about function.
agent_relevance: Functional fixedness is learned, so it grows with knowledge of normal use. This is the human version of the claim that a model trained on typical use will be fixated on typical use.

source: Functional fixedness and cooties (2025): replication of Defeyter and German (2003) in children, abstract via OpenAlex
finding: A direct replication condition reproduced fixedness: children who saw a stick used as a magnet wand were slower to use it to push out a ball than at baseline. A peer demonstration of a different gender fixated less than a same-gender one.
numbers: N=112, 27 per condition, four conditions. Latency to solve slower in all demonstration conditions than baseline. Different-gender peer group faster than same-gender.
limits: Abstract only. Full paper not opened. Child sample and a single apparatus.
agent_relevance: Fixedness replicates in the classic children's paradigm and is socially modulated. Weak link to our agent: the source of the example matters to people, and may not to a model.

source: Fleck and Weisberg (2004) The use of verbal protocols as data: an analysis of insight in the candle problem
finding: On Duncker's candle problem, about one quarter of undergraduates found the box-as-platform solution. Thinking aloud did not change the solution rate. Impasse was not needed for the box solution.
numbers: N=58 (silent vs think-aloud). Box solution about 25% overall (n=13 reported), 27.7% in the silent condition, mean solving time 5.72 min (SD 3.13). Matches the 25% reported by Glucksberg and Weisberg (1966). 44% showed some impasse; only 1 of 34 protocols showed impasse then the box solution.
limits: Verbal overshadowing did not appear, and the authors note that effect is itself unstable. Counts as reported in a lab paper, without a stated effect size.
agent_relevance: A base rate near 25% for the classic task gives a calibration point. Restructuring happened without an impasse, which argues against waiting for a stall before reframing.

source: Howard, Maier, Onarheim and Friis-Olivarius (2013) Overcoming design fixation through education and creativity methods
finding: A short lecture on how the brain makes associations cut the share of designs with copied flawed features. A 'bad ideas' method did not, and cost ideas.
numbers: 12 student teams, three sessions. Fixation ratio .88 (86 designs, 76 fixation elements) before the lecture, .53 after (89 designs, 48 flawed), paired t-test p=.025. Bad Ideas session: 80 designs, 56 flawed (74%), fewer ideas.
limits: Sessions were in a fixed order, so lecture, order and fatigue are confounded. Small teams, one design example. Authors suggest fatigue for the Bad Ideas result.
agent_relevance: Telling the person how the trap works lowered copying. A short stated warning about the specific pull (for example 'your first attempt is anchoring you') is a candidate defixation prompt. Run it counterbalanced.

source: Ward, Patterson, Sifonis, Dodds and Saunders (2002) The role of graded category structure in imaginative thought
finding: When people invent a new animal, tool or fruit, they start from the most easily recalled members of the category. This held even when the task discouraged it or when told to be as creative as possible.
numbers: Accessibility (output dominance, rank) predicted how often an exemplar was named as a starting point (imagination frequency). Held in Exp 2 (constraints against) and Exp 4 (be creative). Typicality and familiarity predicted less well. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Abstract and introduction read. Category-exemplar tasks, student samples.
agent_relevance: Structured imagination predicts the default: new outputs start from the most accessible instance. For an LLM that is the modal output, so ask for and exclude the modal answer first, then generate from the next-ranked one.

source: Deng, Brucks and Toubia (2026) Examining and addressing barriers to diversity in LLM-generated ideas (Study 1)
finding: Within one session, GPT-4o fixates about as much as a person: both add new idea categories at about a third of the possible rate. LLMs are less diverse than humans across sessions, not within one.
numbers: 99 humans vs 99 LLM runs, 10 fitness-product ideas each. Category accumulation slope: human 1.035 vs LLM 1.013 (p=.51), maximum 3.0. Across the group: unique categories 28 human vs 22 LLM; unique combinations 206 vs 88. Within a person: 12.68 vs 12.46 categories (p=.45).
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one product task, online human panel with some signs of outside help. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Fixation in the sequential sense is real in the model: the second idea is pulled by the first. Do not generate a set serially in one context if diversity is the goal.

source: Deng, Brucks and Toubia (2026) (Study 4, chain-of-thought as defixation)
finding: Prompting the model to write short idea titles, then revise them to be bolder and more distinct, then expand them, raised idea diversity. The same procedure did nothing for humans.
numbers: LLM default to CoT: slope 1.013 to 1.363 (p<.001); unique categories 18.45 to 24.84; combinations 39.15 to 55.49; pairwise distance 2.04 to 2.39. Persona+CoT slope .876 to 1.086. Humans: slope 1.035 vs 1.035 (p=.997), categories 26.29 to 25.36. CoT plus ordinary personas beat humans by 26% in diversity.
limits: CoT is a multi-step, higher-token procedure, so not equal compute against a one-shot baseline. No quality scores in the figures read here.
agent_relevance: A plan-then-revise-for-distinctness step raised diversity in the model. Test it against best-of-N at equal tokens (G7) before adding it.

source: Deng, Brucks and Toubia (2026) (Study 3, personas and fixation)
finding: Ordinary personas increased diversity across runs (more knowledge partitioning) but increased fixation inside each run. Famous-entrepreneur personas did not change within-run fixation.
numbers: Between-run distance: ordinary persona M=.635 vs default .241 (2.6 times) vs human .545. Within-run category slope: ordinary persona .876 vs default 1.013. Entrepreneur persona .985 (p=.40 vs default).
limits: Single model. Persona effect depends on persona type. Ten participants per condition for the embedding analysis.
agent_relevance: Persona voters are correlated errors by our G4 and here they also fixate. If used, use them as sampling cues across runs (assigned by code), never as a within-run reasoner.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Verbalized Sampling: how to mitigate mode collapse and unlock LLM diversity
finding: Asking the model to produce a set of answers with stated probabilities restores much of the diversity lost to alignment. The cause they name is a typicality bias in human preference data.
numbers: Creative writing diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting; human rating of diversity +25.7%; recovers 66.8% of the base model's diversity. Larger models gain 1.5 to 2 times more than small models. Gains are additive with temperature. Total compute was held fixed in the comparisons. Baselines include sequence (list of 5) and multi-turn prompts.
limits: Costs more tokens per call and latency, and depends on model scale: small models can lose quality. Read via the HTML copy of version 3.
agent_relevance: A same-compute defixation lever that needs no extra loop: ask for several candidates with probabilities in one call and let code sample from the low-probability ones. Fits G5 (code selects).

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024) The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking (CHI)
finding: People who used an AI image generator for ideas copied more of the starting example than people with no help or with image search, and produced fewer, less varied, less original ideas.
numbers: N=60 between participants, three conditions (baseline, image search, generative AI), 20 minute sketching task, 277 sketches grouped into 83 clusters. Fixation score = features copied from the example / fixating features. Fixation higher with AI; fluency, variety, originality lower than baseline.
limits: Human users with Midjourney, one task (chatbot avatar). Fixation shifted from the example to the AI's images ('fixation displacement'). Test statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Machine-supplied ideas can fixate whoever reads them. An agent reading its own earlier attempts has the same structure.

source: Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of large language models on human creative ideation
finding: Users of ChatGPT and users of a card deck each produced equally homogeneous idea sets as individuals, but the ChatGPT group as a whole converged more.
numbers: Figure caption in the paper: similar individual-level homogeneity for the Oblique Strategies deck and ChatGPT; higher group-level overlap for ChatGPT. Study size and statistics not extracted.
limits: Only the front matter and caption were read. A web-search summary reads the result as 'not individual fixation'; that is not verified here.
agent_relevance: Suggests the collective cost of LLM ideation is across users or runs, not necessarily within a run. Matches Deng et al. Study 1. For one agent, many runs from the same model are one sample of one distribution (G4).

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix: evaluation framework for creative defixation prompting in LLMs
finding: Twenty-five prompts based on creativity and defixation methods (brainstorming, SCAMPER, TRIZ, C-K, design thinking, LLM-specific) beat a control prompt on novelty. No prompt won on every metric, and outputs stayed homogeneous.
numbers: 567 task conditions, 5 models (Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3-30B, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o, Grok-4.1-fast), 3 runs each. All method prompts beat control by t-test. Novelty gains read from a figure: about +10 to +24% on mean novelty; top-5 ideas gained more (up to about +41%). Brainstorming and LLM-specific prompts best; C-K and SCAMPER not clearly better.
limits: Automatic embedding-based novelty and rarity, not human judgment. Percentages are read off a figure and the parse is uncertain. Prompt length differs across methods, so compute is not equal.
agent_relevance: Simple prompt rewording moves novelty a little; complex named methods do not beat simple ones. Keep defixation prompts short. Measure copy rate to the prior attempt, which this paper does not.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a mental set?
finding: Tested Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B and GPT-4o on equivalence problems with a familiar versus a shortcut route. In-context examples raised exact match but did not change the number of reasoning steps.
numbers: Three models, mathematical equivalence set (complex vs shortcut problems). Few-shot + CoT raised exact match for all models; examples helped except in one small-model few-shot cell. Step counts unchanged by in-context examples. Counts not extracted.
limits: Small study, one task family, no human baseline, weak operationalization of 'mental set'. Treat as a pointer, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Shows how thin the direct LLM mental-set literature is. A clean test of our own (prior example vs none, measured copy of method) would be new evidence.

source: Yun et al. (2025) The price of format: diversity collapse in LLMs
finding: Chat-template tokens themselves reduce output diversity on open tasks. The collapse persists under high temperature. The least formatting gave the most diverse outputs.
numbers: Story completion and free-form generation tasks. Specific numbers not extracted. Mixed training with template-free samples gave only marginal improvement over the full template.
limits: Instruction-tuned open models. Effect of format on diversity, not on fixation to a shown example.
agent_relevance: The prompt wrapper affects diversity before any example is shown. Our scaffold's fixed system text may itself be an anchor. Compare minimal vs structured wrappers at equal tokens.

source: Understanding design fixation in generative AI (2025)
finding: A conceptual and qualitative paper defining 'GenAI design fixation' in text and image models and listing mitigation ideas, with participant feedback.
numbers: No effect sizes found in the text read. Participant numbers not extracted.
limits: Framework paper. Weak evidence. Suggested measures (source choice, instructions, interaction design) are untested proposals.
agent_relevance: Useful for vocabulary only. Do not cite it for effect sizes.
